01 - Exploratory data analysis

01_exploratory_analysis.qmd

Overview

This document presents the exploratory data analysis that guided our investigation into the potential existence of trimorphism in Longiperna concolor.

Load data

All data used in this study were collected during a mark-recapture survey conducted between October 2008 and April 2009 by Zatz et al. (2011).

The MALES dataset comprises individual-level information for nearly all L. concolor males marked during the study, including their unique ID and key body measurements: dorsal scute length (DSmm, in mm) and femur length of the fourth right leg (F4mm, in mm). The dataset also includes the morph classifications defined by Zatz et al. (2011).

Note: Our dataset is missing one individual compared to Zatz et al. (2011). Additionally, we chose to ignore the individual 399M, since it appears to be a typo (i.e., it has the largest male dorsal scute length with a very small femur, which seems odd). Therefore, our dataset has 631 males instead of 633, as reported by Zatz et al. (2011).

Exploratory data analysis

The plot below illustrates the morph classification proposed by Zatz et al. (2011), in which major males exhibit longer fourth legs than minor males. In contrast, dorsal scute length shows substantial overlap between morphs, indicating that body size alone does not reliably distinguish them (Fig. 1).

Although males exhibit a unimodal distribution of dorsal scute length (Fig. 1b), the distribution of male femur IV length initially appears bimodal when examined without accounting for morph identity (Fig. 2a). However, once the data are partitioned by male morphs as defined by Zatz et al. (2011), it becomes evident that the distribution within the major morph is itself bimodal (Fig. 2b). This pattern prompted us to investigate the possibility of male trimorphism.

References

Zatz, Camila, Rachel Werneck, Rogelio Macías-Ordóñez, and G. Machado. 2011. “Alternative Mating Tactics in Dimorphic Males of the Harvestman Longiperna Concolor (Arachnida: Opiliones).” Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 65 (May): 995–1005. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00265-010-1103-0.
